events.out:
computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/inness_materials.md (his materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

events.name: read
events.out:
tors are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode). There is no
  `math.atan2`: `math.atan(y, x)` takes two arguments. `%d` in
  `string.format` needs an integer (`7.5` is an error): use `%.0f` or
  `math.floor(x)`. Lists and tables are written with braces:
  `{1, 2}`, `{x = 1}`, never `[1, 2]` or `{x: 1}`.
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Every table walks in a fixed order: booleans, numbers, strings (each
  ascending), then other keys in the order they were made. (Paintings
  begun before engine 3 walk tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans
  in Lua's order.) For a big list, `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** Masks and forms are large: keep big ones `local` when
  later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

nction that isn't zero far
    from the spot you mean paints there too.
45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.
    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting, tacky and touch-dry.
    Drying depends on pigment, thickness and oil; the guide describes
    the times at this easel.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

repainting
  of sold and exhibited works, including scraping with a palette knife
  when the underlying paint was still too wet to rub off. X-radiography confirms major revisions.

## 8. Condition and aging

- **Traction crackle.** "Traction crackle is found in thicker areas of
  brown paint". On one repainted canvas, bitumen or a resin
  addition "probably also caused the considerable traction crackle and
  'crawl' of paint".
- **Abrasion or scraping.** On one canvas "it is difficult to determine
  what is the result of damage and what was intentional scraping by the
  artist during repainting".
- **Cleaning risk.** Restorers in the 1930s damaged one of his canvases
  when they removed his own retouching, mistaking it for old restoration. A well-preserved surface is "somewhat unusual for Inness' work".
- **Old paint showing through.** Cracks in an early canvas reveal a lower
  paint layer.

## 9. The tubes here

The historical names in this note correspond to these tubes: white →
lead white (assumed); black and ivory black → bone black; yellow ocher → yellow
ochre; umber → raw umber; sienna → raw sienna; cadmium → cadmium yellow;
Venetian red → red earth.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with ground layers laid from the tubes.
- **Paint.** Pigment from the tubes with an oil-medium share.
- **Taking paint off.** A brush picks up wet paint as it passes; that is
  how paint comes off the canvas.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

I'm planning the canvas setup—linen ground with lead white and a raw umber stain layer rubbed in Inness's method—then laying out the composition with a horizon line, distant and near tree groups, a reflecting pond, and space for foreground detail.

events.name: note
events.text:
## The idea
A river meadow in late October, about twenty minutes after the sun has gone. I'm standing on a little rise at the edge of a pasture, looking west over low ground. The sky has gone from a cool, smoky gray-blue overhead to a pale lemon and ochre glow just above a far, low tree line. A slow pond, half a meadow wide, lies in the middle distance and holds the last light as a pale bar. A tall group of elms and an oak stands on the right, dark and soft-edged against the glow, their crowns melting into the air. Far off on the left a small farmhouse sits under a few trees, with a thread of smoke. Mist is starting to lift from the low ground in front of the far trees. A woman in a red shawl walks the worn path from the foreground toward the pond: the one warm accent and the reason the place feels lived in. The foreground is dark warm grass, umber and olive, losing its detail in the dusk.

What draws me is the glow caught twice, in the sky and in the water, with the dark masses of the trees and meadow between. I want the edges lost almost everywhere except around the bright water and the figure.

Proportions: 3:2, like his late 30 x 45 canvases. Horizon low, around 0.57 of the height, so the sky gets room. The tree mass sits right of center, the glow and the pond left of center, the figure on the path a little left of the middle where the dark meadow meets the bright water.

Method (after Inness): white lead ground, stained with thin raw umber and rubbed down with a rag. Charcoal-like drawing in a few bold lines. Transparent lay-in thinned with turpentine: raw umber, bone black, raw sienna, scrubbed in, with the lights wiped out with a rag. Let it dry. Then campaigns of opaque, semi-opaque scumbles: the sky in lead white with ochre and lemon, cobalt and black overhead. Trees dragged over the dry sky. Glazes of umber, sienna and black over the foreground. Last, delicate scumbles, mist, the figure's red, and small touches of light.

Since the rag won't help either, the safest fix is waiting for the light patches to fully set, then painting dark treeDark touches back over them—if I paint dark over still-wet light now, it'll just pick the light color back up, so I'll give it two more days.

function dens(x, y)
  local d = 0
  for _, list in ipairs({clE, clL, clR}) do
    for _, c in ipairs(list) do
      local dx, dy = (x-c[1])/c[3], (y-c[2])/(c[3]*0.8)
      local r2 = dx*dx+dy*dy
      if r2 < 4 then d = math.max(d, math.exp(-r2*1.1)) end
    end
  end
  if d > 0.02 then d = d + 0.3*nz(x,y)*math.min(1, d*3) end
  return clamp(d, 0, 1)
end
treeZone = mask(function(x,y) return dens(x,y) > 0.06 and 1 or 0 end)

function massD(x, y)
  local d = 0
  -- left tree skirt, continuous with crown above
  local cl = {{595,365,24},{625,375,26},{660,372,26},{690,368,22},{612,395,20},{650,398,22},{690,396,20},{720,388,18}}
  for _,c in ipairs(cl) do
    local dx, dy = (x-c[1])/c[3], (y-c[2])/(c[3]*0.75)
    local r2 = dx*dx+dy*dy
    if r2 < 4 then d = math.max(d, math.exp(-r2*1.2)) end
  end
  -- far bank line under it
  if x > 552 and x < 735 and y > 396 and y < 416 then
    local e = smoothstep(552, 575, x) * (1 - smoothstep(722, 738, x)) * smoothstep(394, 402, y) * (1 - smoothstep(410, 418, y))
    d = math.max(d, e)
  end
  -- near bush clump at the right block's edge, falling to the shore
  local nb = {{735,400,26},{722,425,22},{745,440,24},{705,440,16},{690,446,12}}
  for _,c in ipairs(nb) do
    local dx, dy = (x-c[1])/c[3], (y-c[2])/(c[3]*0.8)
    local r2 = dx*dx+dy*dy
    if r2 < 4 then d = math.max(d, math.exp(-r2*1.2)) end
  end
  if x > 740 and y > 380 and y < 452 then d = math.max(d, smoothstep(740, 760, x)) end
  d = d + 0.3*nz(x,y)*math.min(1,d*3)
  return clamp(d,0,1)
end
massZone = mask(function(x,y) if x < 540 or x > 780 or y < 340 or y > 462 then return 0 end; return massD(x,y) > 0.07 and 1 or 0 end)
local core = mask(function(x,y) if x < 540 or x > 780 or y < 340 or y > 462 then return 0 end; return massD(x,y) > 0.6 and 1 or 0 end)

I'm realizing the patchwork approach is the real issue; the whole right side needs a unified method, maybe glazing the tree and bush area dark first and then wiping out highlights, Inness-style, rather than building up separate textured blocks.

The pond's reflection will get a dark band painted with blended horizontal strokes where the mass meets the water, and I'll stipple the crown transitions while everything is still wet to keep it cohesive.

events.text:
This is getting messy—the rim is flat while the interior has texture, which is backwards. I should step back and consider a radical simplification inspired by Inness's late style, where trees become soft, blurred masses rather than leafy texture. The stipple approach might be a liability; better to make the whole grove one smoothly modulated dark mass.

My plan: paint the sky band wet around the tree first, then the tree mass wet with olive-lit variation and a dark core, then blend the rim edge while both are still wet to create a soft transition—true wet-into-wet. After it dries, I can glaze, add lit scumbles, show trunks lower down, and paint a few sky holes with small strokes. I also want to redesign the silhouette to be more elm-like with irregular lobes and a gap between trees, keeping it close to the existing grove shape.

Since dark is already there, covering it with sky requires opaque paint, which the lead-white-rich sky mix handles fine in two coats. I'll define the silhouette using a density function from the clump shapes, thresholded and smoothed for lobed edges, with the sky ring filling the grove region outside it. For the wet blending at the boundary, badgering dark and light together while both are wet should produce the soft Inness-style halo I saw working in the day-100 version—the earlier problem was holes, not the blending technique itself. I'll set varying tree heights (tall elm center-right, smaller left tree, right edge tree) and extend the repaint down to include the bush band, which is already dry but has some gray speckling from the veil.

events.text: Day 241: the gray veil around the crowns left a moldy halo, and the dark stippling I put back over it made a flat rim with loose "leaves" floating outside. Looking at it whole: the trouble is texture. My crowns are leaf-textured and Inness's are not. They are broad, softly modulated masses, and their edges come from painting the sky and the dark together, wet into wet, and blending across the junction. Next I do exactly that in one sitting: the sky ring around the grove, then the whole grove mass in body color with olive light on the glow side and a cool dark core, then blend across the edge. Holes and trunks come later, over dry paint.

events.text:
Looking at the composition critically, I realize it's weak overall—the meadow is flat and the path barely reads, while the grove's two holes accidentally create an unsettling face-like symmetry with eye-shaped gaps. I need to step back and rethink the whole piece, starting by breaking up that eye-like symmetry in the grove.

For fixes: fill the left hole mostly, leaving small flickers, and widen the big gap lower with trunks crossing through it to read as light filtering under a canopy, as Inness often painted. The grove's silhouette also needs a less rounded, more irregular top with subsidiary masses and softened stippled edges. The meadow needs darker glazing overall for a dusk feel, with the path reading as lighter worn earth and a strip of sky-light catching the near bank—right now it's too bright and greenish. The pond's edge is also too hard and uniform and needs breaking up.

The pond also needs a glowing reflection gradient that echoes the sky—lemon far side, grayer near—with soft edges and dark reflected shapes from the grove at the right. Figure, house, and smoke can wait. The sky is mostly fine but the top-left feels bland, so I might add a soft rose-gray cloud bank. I'll glaze the meadow and fix the grove in this sitting since they're dry and separate areas.

Glaze the meadow much darker (umber, black, a little Antwerp) and wipe the light back on the path and the near-shore strip. Give the pond a glow gradient and soft dark reflections of the grove. events.text:
The patchwork approach is making the boxy seams visible, so I'm fighting the medium instead of working with it. Better to abandon this piecemeal fixing and commit to a single unifying final pass, Inness-style, covering the whole surface wet-into-wet in one sitting with masks guided by drawn contours and tonal blending.

My plan is to redo everything below y=330 while leaving the sky alone: fix the lower grove and bank, repaint the field beyond the pond, redo the water with its glow and reflection, and finish the meadow, all painted to natural edges rather than hard-edged rectangular patches to avoid the box-seam problem. I should let the current layer dry first before starting this full campaign, since painting wet-into-wet now would just cause unwanted mixing.

For the remaining effort, I should focus on giving the tree more internal structure—lighter olive-gray masses facing the glow, a few dark accents, a visible trunk through the mist at the bottom, and a broken, irregular silhouette edge to feel more Inness-like.

I'll leave the silhouette mostly intact but add small dark foliage protrusions across the top edge, since stippling dark over dry sky worked well before. The yellow crust can be covered with opaque sky paint carefully masked to a ring outside the tree, similar to what worked on an earlier pass, then softened with light outward blending and a few feathered dark touches crossing the edge.

The gray-mix blend is physically correct but the band is way too wide for this scale—about 11mm when a real lost edge should be just a few millimeters at most.

I'm also seeing the band read as a cool, lighter halo outline rather than a soft merge, plus visible seams where the patch meets the painted interior. Rather than chase perfection pixel by pixel, I'll let things dry and apply a unified glaze over the whole grove area—including the band—to darken the transition toward the tree and smooth over the seams so it reads as one cohesive soft edge.

The crackle texture from the glaze over dry paint isn't quite ideal, but at viewing distance it reads as a textured dark mass, so it's acceptable. I'm also noting the pale halo of thick, lighter paint around the left tree where it meets the sky band.

Thinking it over, trying to patch just the halo zone risks blotching like earlier scumble attempts did. The better move is to let everything dry fully, then redo the entire sky in one broad sitting the way I did on day 252, since that approach gave the best, most cohesive result — then handle the grove edge afterward with stippled dark foliage over the dry sky and a final unifying glaze on the grove itself.

I'm planning to repaint the whole sky except the shrink mask in one broad pass, then darken the grove edge band to meet the wet area and blend a narrow tangent line lightly, accepting some minor grayness. I'm also realizing the lose operation on the mask could accidentally affect the canvas edge and bottom meadow area, so I need to restrict it more carefully.

events.text:
The grove reads as too smooth and blob-like, more like a rock or mushroom than Inness-style trees, which usually have soft masses but still some differentiation — distinct trunks, silhouette variety, light breaking through. I'm noticing the grove's hard edge at the top-left with flecks, a flat gray mist band below that reads like a wall, an overly flat olive meadow, and a uniformly gray-violet far tree line that lacks variation.

To fix this I'm planning to break the grove into distinct tree forms with varied silhouette lobes, darken the base with glimpses of trunk, add warm reddish-brown texture to the meadow with darker foreground corners and lighter zones near water, include a few small accents like a red-coated figure or smoke from a house, and add warm cloud streaks to the sky. I want to work efficiently now since there have already been many iterations — I'll paint sky-colored notches into the dry grove silhouette to separate the tree crowns, starting with a dip in the elm's top.

I'm realizing the sky-holes need to be small and edge-positioned, tinted close to the sky color rather than pure white, so they read as translucent foliage gaps instead of harsh dots — I'll try careful sizing at the edges. The hair-like dark flecks at the top edge look fine from a distance, so I'll leave those. Stepping back, the overall composition reads okay at scale, so I'm prioritizing the grove base, meadow modulation, the figure, house, clouds, and some tree differentiation with a lighter warm olive on the lower tree's left side plus a visible trunk — but I need to wait for the water to dry and confirm the grove base is dry enough to work on.

events.name: paint
events.code:
twigP = pile{{"raw umber",2},{"bone black",1.2}, medium=0.2}
local gs = GS:mask()
local cnt = 0
local rb = brush{kind="rigger", width=1.6, point=1}
for _, a in ipairs(uneven(70, 0, 1, 0.6, 0.5, 211)) do
  local px, py = GS:at(a)
  if py < 300 and px < 1000 and px > 600 then
    local qx, qy = GS:at(math.min(1, a + 0.002))
    local tx, ty = qx-px, qy-py
    local len = math.sqrt(tx*tx+ty*ty) + 1e-6
    local nx, ny = -ty/len, tx/len
    if gs:at(px+nx*6, py+ny*6) > 0.5 then nx, ny = -nx, -ny end
    local ang = math.atan(ny, nx) + rand(-0.5, 0.5)
    -- bias upward
    if math.sin(ang) > 0.3 then ang = ang - 0.6 end
    local L = rand(8, 20)
    local sx, sy = px - nx*3, py - ny*3
    local mx, my = sx + math.cos(ang)*L*0.5 + rand(-2,2), sy + math.sin(ang)*L*0.5 + rand(-2,2)
    local ex, ey = sx + math.cos(ang)*L, sy + math.sin(ang)*L
    rb:load(twigP, 0.6)
    rb:stroke({{sx,sy},{mx,my},{ex,ey}}, {pressure={0.55,0.0}, ramps={0.05,0.8}})
    if math.random() < 0.6 then
      local ba = ang + rand(-0.8, 0.8)
      rb:stroke({{mx,my},{mx+math.cos(ba)*L*0.45, my+math.sin(ba)*L*0.45}}, {pressure={0.35,0.0}, ramps={0.05,0.8}})
    end
    cnt = cnt + 1
  end
end
print(cnt)

events.text:
## Reflection, day 614
The finished picture: a lemon-to-violet dusk sky over a hazy far tree line with a farmhouse and a thread of smoke. A pale pond holds the glow, with the grove's reflection bleeding into it on the right. The big dark grove on the right melts into mist at its foot. A dark meadow is glazed in umber and black, with a worn track, and a small woman in a red shawl stands where the path meets the lighter ground by the water. She came out well: the one warm note, and the scale of the place.

What works: the sky's gradient, the far distance, the pond, and the figure against the near-shore light. The meadow's glaze settles in the hollows of the knife-textured ground like stubble at dusk. The pale bloom of air left of the grove reads as light behind the trees.
What doesn't: the grove is still too much one heavy, hard-edged silhouette. Inness would have let more air into it and dissolved the edges. It shows the record of many repairs (stipple ring, olive dry-brush texture). Above all I learned the easel's physics the hard way: rectangular blends over contrasting wet paint, opaque scumbles that turn into blotches, and a rag that won't lift tacky paint. If I painted it again I would build the trees from the start as broad, thin, transparent masses over the stain and keep them thin until the end, wiping lights out instead of adding opaque ones.
Signed lower right.

**Evening, the River Meadow**

This is a late-October dusk on a 3:2 canvas, about twenty minutes after sunset. The sky runs from a smoky violet-gray overhead down to a pale lemon glow over a hazy far tree line. In that tree line a small farmhouse shows a lit window and a thin trail of smoke. Below it a still pond catches the last light. On the right a big dark grove of elms runs down into mist at the water's edge, and its reflection bleeds into the pond. In front is a dark meadow glazed with umber, black and a little Antwerp blue, with a worn track crossing it. A small woman in a red shawl stands where the track meets the lighter ground by the water. She is the one warm note in the picture and gives it its scale.

I worked the way the notes say Inness did. I stained the white-lead ground with raw umber and rubbed it back with a rag, drew in chalk, and laid in thin, turpentine-thinned paint, wiping the lights of the pond and the path out with a rag. After that came many campaigns over about 600 simulated days. Opaque sky and meadow layers went on, then dark glazes left to dry between sessions. Twice I covered the trees completely with sky paint and started them again ("plastering the wall").

The sky, the far distance, the pond and the figure work best. The grove is the weak part. It's still too heavy and too sharp-edged against the sky, Inness would have let more air into it, and you can see the layers of my repairs on it. I've signed it lower right.

tors are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode). There is no
  `math.atan2`: `math.atan(y, x)` takes two arguments. `%d` in
  `string.format` needs an integer (`7.5` is an error): use `%.0f` or
  `math.floor(x)`. Lists and tables are written with braces:
  `{1, 2}`, `{x = 1}`, never `[1, 2]` or `{x: 1}`.
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Every table walks in a fixed order: booleans, numbers, strings (each
  ascending), then other keys in the order they were made. (Paintings
  begun before engine 3 walk tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans
  in Lua's order.) For a big list, `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** Masks and forms are large: keep big ones `local` when
  later chunks don't need them.

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what

local g = newG
local count = 0
clumpAll = nil
local function addClumps(o, n, seed, rmin, rmax, out)
  for i, t in ipairs(uneven(n, 0, 1, 0.7, 0.5, seed)) do
    local px, py = o:at(t)
    local qx, qy = o:at((t + 0.003) % 1)
    local tx, ty = qx-px, qy-py
    local L = math.sqrt(tx*tx+ty*ty) + 1e-6
    local nx, ny = ty/L, -tx/L
    if g:at(px+nx*6, py+ny*6) > 0.5 then nx, ny = -nx, -ny end
    if g:at(px+nx*12, py+ny*12) < 0.5 and py < 392 and px < 1000 then
      local r = rand(rmin, rmax)
      local cx, cy = px + nx*rand(0, out)*r/10, py + ny*rand(0, out)*r/10
      -- drooping: shift down a bit on the sides
      cy = cy + rand(0, 3)
      local pts = {}
      local k = 7
      for j = 1, k do
        local a = (j-1)/k*2*math.pi + rand(-0.3,0.3)
        local rr = r * rand(0.6, 1.1)
        table.insert(pts, {cx + math.cos(a)*rr*1.15, cy + math.sin(a)*rr*0.85})
      end
      pts.closed = true; pts.char = "soft"; pts.seed = seed*100+i; pts.lobe = 3; pts.amount = 1.0
      local m = outline(pts):mask()
      clumpAll = clumpAll and (clumpAll + m) or m
      count = count + 1
    end
  end
end

events.text:
## Reflection, day 739
I came back to the grove, the one thing I'd left unresolved. I drew it again as four separate masses: the elm crown, the right-hand tree, the left tree on the far bank, and the understory. I plastered the old silhouette with sky and repainted the whole sky in one sitting, cut against the new shapes. Then I laid each mass wet into wet: a dark body, olive light on the glow side, cool sky light on the tops, a deep core, and broken clumps along the edges, blended along the contour. Over the dry paint I opened a real gap under the elm's canopy, with the glow seen through it, crossed by the elm's trunk and its forking limbs, a sapling, the right tree's trunk and low bushes in haze. That gap is the change I like most. The grove is now trees with sky behind them, not one lump, and it echoes the light in the pond. I also put a last glaze over the meadow to settle the light column at x 510–580, and softened the seam at the foot of the grove into mist.

What still isn't Inness: the edges of the crowns are scalloped where they should be dissolved, and the right-hand tree is still a heavy block. But my heart is content with the place: the lemon glow, the pale water, the dark trees with the light under them, and the small red figure walking toward it all. I'm leaving it here.

I'm calling it **"October Dusk, the Meadow Pond"**, and I'm happy to leave it here.

The scene is a lemon-to-violet sky about twenty minutes after sunset, over a hazy far tree line with a farmhouse and a thread of smoke. A pale pond holds the last light, and a dark meadow glazed in umber leads up a worn track to a small woman in a red shawl at the water's edge.

**What changed this session**
- **The grove.** I'd left it unresolved last time. I covered the old silhouette with sky and repainted the whole sky in one sitting. Then I redrew the grove as separate trees, an elm, a right-hand tree, a tree on the far bank and low growth beneath them, and painted each mass wet into wet, with olive light on the side facing the glow and cool light along the tops.
- **The opening under the elm.** Once the paint was dry, I opened a gap under the elm's canopy so the glow shows through, crossed by its trunk and forked limbs, a sapling and a few hazy bushes. I like this change most: the grove now reads as trees with sky behind them, and that light under the trees echoes the light in the pond.
- **The meadow.** A last glaze settled a pale column in the foreground left over from an earlier patch, and I softened a hard seam at the foot of the grove into mist.

**What still falls short of Inness**
- The edges of the tree crowns are scalloped where his would dissolve into the air.
- The right-hand tree is still a heavy block.

My reflections are in the journal.

## Reflection, day 760
A short last visit. I dragged thinned dark paint across the crown edges with `lose` to break up the scalloped rim. In places it now reads as twigs and air, though it's still not Inness's dissolve. I wiped off some stray hatched streaks in the sky right of the elm, and glazed the bottom of the meadow and the band beyond the figure darker. That leaves the light ground around her and the near shore as the one lit place in the field, which pulls the eye down the path to her and the water. I lifted a dark bump that had crept onto the far field at the left edge, and a band along the pond's right shore, with a rag in spirits while they were still open. One more lesson: a glaze brushed over the whole grove left horizontal stripes. Over dry paint a spirit-rag took nearly all of it back off, which is the closest thing this easel has to an undo. The picture is the same place it was and a little quieter. I'm content to leave it.

I've finished the painting and given it the title **October Dusk, the Pond Meadow**.

The time is about twenty minutes after sundown. A lemon glow fades upward into violet-gray over a hazy far tree line, where a small farmhouse sends up a thread of smoke. A pale pond in the middle distance holds the last of that light. On the right a grove of elms stands dark against the glow, with the bright sky showing through a gap under the main crown. Across the dark, glazed meadow a worn path leads to a small woman in a red shawl near the water. She is the one warm note in the picture and gives it its scale.

In this last visit I softened the crowns' scalloped edges by dragging thinned dark paint out across them. I also glazed the bottom of the meadow and the field past her darker, so the patch of light around her and the near shore is the brightest part of the field.

Two things went wrong. A glaze I brushed over the whole grove left horizontal stripes, and I took almost all of it back off with a rag dipped in spirits. A rag wiped over some stray streaks in the sky right of the elm barely lifted them, because that paint had already dried.

The crown edges still don't dissolve into the sky the way Inness's would. But I'm happy with the place: the light caught twice, in the sky and the water, and the small figure walking toward it.

This visit was short:
- **Right-hand tree:** I took the pale streaks out and stippled a little dark over the dry paint, so the tree now reads as quiet shadow.
- **Left meadow:** I tried an opaque olive band near the shore, and it went down as a flat patch. It took many passes with a rag dipped in spirits to lift it, and a slight warm tint is left over the texture. This is the third time opaque paint over the textured meadow has turned into a patch; only transparent glazes work there.
- **Final glaze:** A graded transparent glaze darkens the left meadow from the shore toward the foreground. The field now rolls down into shadow, and the lit ground stays by the water and around the figure.

The crown edges are still more scalloped than Inness would have left them. Still, the glow caught twice, in the sky and in the water, with the dark trees between, is the place I set out to paint. My reflections are in the journal.
